description: An audiogram from the DHS Blue Campaign '#TacklingTrafficking' series: a static blue graphic with a play icon and audio-waveform animation plays a recorded clip of Forensic Interview Specialist Lauren G. saying that trafficking victims are typically groomed rather than kidnapped, with her words shown as text-card captions. There is no video footage and no music, only narrated interview audio over a fixed graphic. | Unlike what is portrayed in the media, trafficking victims are groomed by the trafficker and not necessarily randomly kidnapped. It is not out of the realm of possibility, however, and there have been known cases of individuals being kidnapped because they began to uncover the trafficker's scheme and decide they no longer wanted to be a part of it, so they are taken by force and held against their will. But that typically happens after the victim has been in the situation for some time. So this is another myth which has been around for many years as it was the thing to look for when kidnappings first started making way into the lives of so many families here in the United States. | Reviewed video keyframe (direct frame analysis); media form recorded via the candidate tag

tweet_text: This is what generational change looks like. Yesterday, U.S. Coast Guard Cutter (USCGC) Storis transited the Panama Canal, marking a significant milestone on its maiden voyage towards its future homeport in Juneau. After departing the Panama Canal, Storis met three recently decommissioned 110’ Island-Class Patrol Boats from Alaska – USCGCs Liberty, Mustang, and Naushon. These are the last of the storied 110’s, being succeeded by the modern Sentinel-class Fast Response Cutters. Today’s passage exemplifies the Coast Guard’s transformation under Force Design 2028. As the United States’ third polar icebreaker, Storis will bring innovative capabilities and crewing to assure access to the polar regions and protect U.S. sovereignty. The Key Bridge collapse underscored the significance of America’s Marine Transportation System, our vital network of ports and waterways. As efforts continue toward rebuilding the Key Bridge, the Coast Guard is steadfast in our resolve to respond to contingencies and facilitate commerce vital to economic prosperity.

On May 31, a Jacksonville Air and Marine Branch Multi-Role Enforcement Aircraft detected a surface target of interest about 65 nautical miles south of the Turks and Caicos Islands (TCI). Air Interdiction Agents relayed information to TCI authorities and OPBAT partners, providing updated position, course, and speed reports. The AMO aircrew conducted a successful over-the-air handoff of the STOI to a U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) aircraft. USCG aircrew reported the vessel had lost one engine, was slowly taking on water, and occupants were observed bailing 3–5 gallons of water per minute. At approximately 9:00 pm, USCG reported the vessel was dead in the water and occupants continued to bail water using buckets. TCI authorities declared a search and rescue case due to increased risk of capsizing and launched four maritime surface assets. At approximately 1:00 a.m. on June 1, TCI authorities successfully rescued/interdicted the STOI. TCI authorities reported a total of 240 migrants onboard: 191 adult males, 44 adult females, and 5 minors. The passengers and crew were taken by Turks and Caicos authorities and did not reach U.S. soil.
